prize_parts.citation: for evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: I move my first preference from B017 to B044. The reason is not the support counts but the scientific arguments colleagues raised about overlap and attribution. The China-shock papers by Autor, Dorn and Hanson rest on a transparent and widely replicated research design. They show that import competition causes persistent employment, wage and adjustment losses in exposed local labour markets. This changed trade and labour economics, and it also changed how the profession and policymakers think about the distributional and political consequences of globalisation. Autor's task-based work on polarisation supplies the labour-demand framework. The two strands share one question, which is how technology and trade shift labour demand, so a single citation can cover them. The identification is more credible than in most cross-country work. The core papers are over a decade old, with extensive replication across countries and many refinements. Those refinements have qualified the magnitudes but have not overturned the finding of long-lasting local costs. On the common criteria of influence, credibility and maturity, I rate it among the strongest candidates. Its attribution is also easier to defend than that of most larger groupings, because the three named authors jointly wrote the central trade-shock papers.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize would join two strands that could be judged separately. The task-based framework has a lineage that includes Autor-Levy-Murnane, Acemoglu and Katz, and some of those people are outside this credited set or already recognised. The trade-shock strand is mainly empirical and relies on shift-share instruments, whose inference problems and effect sizes are still debated. It is also more recent than most older candidates, so the long-run persistence of the effects is still being assessed. A Committee could reasonably prefer a candidate with a single conceptual breakthrough and cleaner attribution, such as the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism.

responses.point: Hassler sees the task-based approach and the trade-shock empirics as separable strands shared among Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Katz. He proposes Autor and Hanson as the most defensible pair, with Dorn and Katz as plausible alternatives.
responses.response: I agree the two strands are separable and that the attribution involves judgement. I do not agree that Dorn is the natural one to drop. He co-authored the central China-shock papers with Autor and Hanson. Leaving him out would be harder to defend on attribution than including him, and the three-name limit allows it. Katz's contribution is the earlier skill-biased change literature, which sits better in a different citation. So I keep the trio tied to the trade-shock and labour-demand evidence, and I accept that this narrows the credit given to the task framework.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first and proposes Autor, Katz and Hanson. She argues that technology, tasks and wage inequality are tied to Autor and Katz, while the trade shock is tied to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. She notes that a three-person award covering both strands leaves out Dorn.
responses.response: This is the clearest statement of the attribution problem, and I take it seriously. If the prize rested on the skill-bias and task lineage, Katz would be indispensable. I read the case as resting more on the credible local-labour-market evidence and the labour-demand framework that frames it. On that reading Dorn belongs and Katz is better left to the broader inequality literature. I am less sure than she is that both strands can be honoured in three names. That uncertainty is why I name B040 as an alternative, where the attribution is cleaner.

responses.point: Krusell treats Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the clear core authors of the trade-shock work. He sees the task-based strand as a separate line that overlaps with Acemoglu, who is already recognised. He also raises possible overlap with the 2024 prize.
responses.response: I agree with his attribution and it shapes my citation. The 2024 prize concerned the causal effect of inclusive institutions on long-run prosperity. The China-shock work concerns local labour-market adjustment to a trade shock, which is a different mechanism and a different object of identification. I share his caution about the task framework, so the citation should not claim the whole technology-and-inequality literature. I concede the point is open on the task strand, because the Committee might want it attributed more broadly.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B017 third and flags that the 2024 institutions prize may reduce its marginal appeal. He also asks whether the task framework and the trade-shock work are one prize-sized contribution or two.
responses.response: On B017 he is right, and his point moved me. The 2024 prize makes a political-economy award this soon harder to justify, even though electoral rules and fiscal capacity are different mechanisms from those in the 2024 work. That is why I demote it to an alternative. On his second question, I think the shared labour-demand question supports one prize. That is a judgement and not a settled fact, and I regard it as the main unresolved issue for B044.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B040 first and argues that the Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles paper is the clear originating contribution, so a two-person award is the cleanest attribution. He acknowledges possible overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I accept that B040 has the cleanest attribution of the leading candidates, and that is why I list it as an alternative. On overlap, the 2022 prize concerned banks and financial crises, while Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral constraints and asset prices propagate shocks. Those are distinct enough that I do not treat the overlap as disqualifying. My reservation is that the mechanism has more indirect empirical validation than the quasi-experimental evidence in B044. I weigh that against B044's less clean attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the task-based framework and the China-shock evidence should be treated as one prize-sized achievement or two, and whether Katz belongs in a version that credits the task strand.
How persistent and how large the trade-shock effects are under alternative identification and inference approaches for shift-share designs.
Whether the Committee would see the contribution as mainly empirical findings rather than a conceptual breakthrough, and whether it is mature enough given that the core papers date from about 2013.
Whether B040 would be preferred on attribution grounds once the 2022 overlap is weighed.
My assessment relies on general knowledge and the supplied materials, not independent verification of citations or impact figures.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B044, B040 or the other shortlisted candidates. The profile lists collaborators and institutional ties (V-Dem core team, Rothstein, Holmberg, Hadenius, Dahlström, Lapuente, Bäck, Lindvall) but none are credited names on the shortlist. His Stockholm University colleagues on the committee (Hassler, Krusell, Boppart) are in a different department. As a political scientist I note field proximity to B017, now an alternative, and I do not treat it as a recusal basis.
